Swifter
swift'-ēr
adj. (comparative of swift: faster; of eagles, shuttles, posts and invading horses)
From swift, Saxon swift. Every occurrence in the Authorized Version is a comparison, and the things compared are worth listing: eagles, leopards, a weaver's shuttle and a running post. Speed in Scripture is measured against creatures and against the working day.

Biblical Definition

Job twice measures his life by the fastest things he knows. “My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope” (Job 7:6) — a shuttle crosses the loom faster than the eye follows, and the thread runs out. “Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good” (Job 9:25); the post is the royal courier, the fastest man in the kingdom. That is Scripture's picture of a human life from the inside, and it is not softened. David uses the word in the lament over Saul and Jonathan: “they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions” (2Sa 1:23) — generous words for a king who had hunted him for years, spoken over his corpse. The prophets use it of the coming invader, and they use the same eagle: Jeremiah's Babylonian horses are “swifter than eagles” (Jer 4:13), Habakkuk's Chaldean horses “swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves” (Hab 1:8), and Lamentations says of the fall itself, “Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven” (Lam 4:19). Judgment, when it finally comes after generations of warning, arrives faster than anyone expected.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines swift as moving with great speed or velocity, fleet, rapid, quick; and notes its Scriptural use for that which passes rapidly away.

expand to see more

SWIFT, a. Moving a great distance or over a large space in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy.

1. Ready; prompt. Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak. James 1.

2. Of short continuance; passing with celerity.

POST, n. A messenger or a carrier of letters and papers; one who travels with expedition.

Key Scripture

Job 7:6 — "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope."

Job 9:25 — "Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good."

2Sa 1:23 — "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions."

Hab 1:8 — "Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat."

Modern Corruption

Mortality is managed out of sight; Job holds a shuttle and a courier up against his own days and will not look away.

expand to see more

Our arrangements are built to keep the shortness of life out of consciousness — the sick moved out of the home, the dead handled by professionals, the language of age euphemized, the calendar filled. Job says the thing plainly and Scripture prints it: my days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle. It is not morbid; it is the necessary precondition of wisdom, which is why Moses prays to be taught to number his days and the psalmist asks to know his end. A man who has never reckoned honestly with the speed of the shuttle will spend his life on things that cannot survive it.

David's lament deserves the second word, because it shows what a believer may do with a bitter history. Saul had thrown spears at him, hunted him through the wilderness, and slaughtered the priests of Nob for helping him. Over his body David sings that Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. He does not falsify the record — he simply refuses to settle accounts with a dead man. That is not sentimentality; it is the ninth commandment kept toward an enemy, and it is rare enough to be worth naming.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qalal (H7043), to be light, hence swift; 'ereg (H708), a weaver's shuttle; nesher (H5404), eagle.

expand to see more

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, and so to be swift; Job 7:6, 9:25, 2 Samuel 1:23.

Hebrew 'ereg (H708) — a weaver's shuttle or loom; Job 7:6, the only such use in Scripture.

Hebrew nesher (H5404) — eagle (or great vulture); the standard measure of speed in the prophets.

Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; the root behind post, the royal runner of Job 9:25.

Greek tachus (G5036) — swift, quick; James 1:19, swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.

Usage

"“Swifter than a weaver's shuttle” — and the thread runs out."

"“Swifter than a post: they flee away” — the fastest man in the kingdom."

"“They were swifter than eagles” — said of the king who hunted him."
